A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InteractComp benchmark, with matching construction principles, dataset coverage and original experiments. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 17 models, configuration ablations, round-budget experiments and forced-interaction results in Tables 2–4 and Appendix A.5.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds interaction ablations, responder validation, commercial-system evaluations and analyses of failures, ranking consistency and interaction usefulness.

M1.justification: The target-distractor construction and core ReAct architecture remain. v2 introduces limited procedural variants: Answer+Interact removes search from the available actions, and askNL permits free-form responder answers instead of three-way responses (Sections 4.1 and 4.5). These extend the implementation without replacing the main method.

E1.justification: Both versions use 210 ambiguous identification questions across nine domains, comprising 139 English and 71 Chinese instances. Added studies reuse these questions or their interaction records. The new agent and responder configurations change evaluation procedures within the retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix B.3 adds evaluated comparisons with Doubao Deep Search and OpenAI Deep Research. These commercial systems are additional comparators, distinct from the retained 17-model suite, including Doubao-1.6. No original model comparator is removed.

E3.justification: v2 adds ten-round ask-only and free-form-response configurations, matched-responder comparisons on 50 questions, human validation of 100 interaction records by two annotators, and interaction-utility measurements on 50 questions. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The main ten-round configuration and stated sampling parameters remain unchanged; the additions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original configuration, scaling and forced-interaction analyses are retained. v2 adds tests of search removal, response-channel restrictions, responder sensitivity and human agreement, scaffold dependence, and interaction usefulness. Section 4.7 and Appendix C.2 additionally provide failure attribution and a case where clarification and search still produce Ice Hockey instead of Hornussen.

E5.justification: The original main-table standard deviations and three-trial responder sampling remain. v2 newly identifies three independent main runs and reports pairwise Kendall rank correlations with p-values in Table B2. Appendix B.2 adds Krippendorff’s alpha and Cohen’s kappa for simulator–human agreement. This substantially expands statistical validation without establishing an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Original main-table values and the complete scaling/forced-interaction appendix results are unchanged. Substantial new results include GPT-5 accuracy of 25.24% with ask-only and 25.71% with askNL, commercial-system accuracies of 10.0% and 6.67%, and responder, agreement, ranking, utility and failure-attribution findings. These are additional results under their respective settings, not revisions demonstrating same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The construction mathematics and responder-state formulation are retained, with no new theoretical results or proofs. Appendix A.6 supplies the standard five-bin expected-calibration-error formula for the already-used metric; this is additional explanation rather than a theoretical contribution.

C1.justification: The three principal contributions, headline performance gap and longitudinal-stagnation claim remain. v2 qualifies broad statements about complete-query assumptions and adds a conclusion that richer natural-language feedback alone does not close the performance gap. These refine the claims without redefining the paper’s central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the earlier overconfidence diagnosis and brief model-specific caveats into a strategic-versus-tactical account: deciding when to interact versus identifying useful questions. It adds interpretations of response bandwidth and interaction utility, explains the diagnostic purpose of restricted replies, cautions against fine-grained rankings, and explicitly treats simulated feedback as an approximation to real users.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents Serper search with five organic results and a 30-second timeout, annotator qualifications and paraphrase checks, a candidate-refinement threshold, configuration details, and confidence parsing. Conversely, it removes v1’s grader identity, temperature, human spot-check statement and complete grading prompt. These substantially change reproducibility documentation; the code-access link remains.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands coverage of earlier ambiguity and clarification research, including AmbigQA, ASQA and clarification-question studies. It repositions InteractComp as complementary through its search/ask/answer loop, rather than relying primarily on a general-conversation versus search distinction. It also adds connections to tip-of-the-tongue retrieval, real-user query datasets and agent-training research.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much original prose remain. Changes include localized abstract, introduction and conclusion rewrites, expanded explanations, an Impact Statement, and reorganization into Appendices A–C. Author and venue/header text are also updated; the revision is not a pervasive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, adds an interaction-workflow diagram and several tables, moves the original task example to Appendix A.1, expands the ablation table, transposes the scaling table and rearranges the dataset-statistics figure. The revised forced-interaction plot omits GPT-4o-mini, although its numerical results remain in Appendix C.1.

improvement.justification: v1 left important alternative explanations insufficiently tested, including restricted response bandwidth, simulator choice and the ReAct scaffold. v2 directly examines these issues and adds human validation and detailed failure analysis, substantially strengthening the benchmark’s empirical validity and diagnostic value. The broader clarification literature also improves its positioning. Removing grader details weakens reproducibility, but the added validation and explanation provide a clear, substantial net improvement.
